PMU Measurement Based Generator Parameter
Calibration by Black-Box Optimization with A
Stochastic Radial Basis Function Surrogate Model
Seyyed Rashid Khazeiynasab and Junjian Qi
Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
University of Central Florida
Orlando, FL 32816 USA
Emails: rashid@knights.ucf.edu; junjianqi@ieee.org
Abstract—In this paper, we propose a synchrophasor mea-
surement based generator parameter calibration method by a
black-box optimization approach with a stochastic radial basis
function (RBF) surrogate model. Based on comparison between
the outputs of the generator model with estimated parameters
and the phasor measurement unit (PMU) measurements, we
deﬁne an objective function for the black-box optimization
problem, which is approximated by a RBF surrogate model. The
prior information of the parameters is treated as constraints in
the black-box optimization problem. The formulated black-box
optimization problem is then solved by a Stochastic Response
Surface Method (MSRSM). The effectiveness of the proposed
method is tested and validated on a hydro generator. The sim-
ulation results show that the proposed approach can accurately
and efﬁciently estimate the generator parameters subject to gross
errors in the prior distributions of the parameters.
Index Terms—Black-box optimization, dynamic parameter
estimation, global optimization, parameter calibration, phasor
measurement unit (PMU), power system dynamics, radial basis
function, sensitivity analysis, synchrophasor.
I. I NTRODUCTION
Because power system monitoring, protection, and control
are usually model based, an accurate dynamic model for
synchronous generators is essential for a valid evaluation of
the system dynamic performance [1]–[3]. Different approaches
have been proposed for generator model validation and pa-
rameter calibration. Ofﬂine methods based on ﬁeld tests, such
as standstill frequency response method [4] and open circuit
frequency response method [5], involve physical testing of the
generator under a variety of physical and electrical conditions
corresponding to simulated grid-connected events. Because the
generator has to be out of service during physical testing,
ofﬂine methods are not economically viable [6].
To overcome the deﬁciencies of the ofﬂine methods, online
methods have been proposed, in which a known model for
the generator is considered and the physical parameters are
estimated based on online measurements [7]. With the recent
advancement of phasor measurement unit (PMU) technologies,
there is an increasing interest in estimating the synchronous
generator parameters using synchrophasor data, which has
been proven to be a cost efﬁcient alternative. The PMU
measurements based online methods can more accurately
capture real operating ranges and operational relationships
between the generator and the grid than stand-alone testing
of individual physical generators. The methods proposed in
[8], [9] use a hybrid dynamic simulation. The errors between
the model outputs and the PMU data are calculated for each
step and the parameters are estimated based on the minimum
errors. However, the iterative dynamic simulation in these
methods is time-consuming [10]. The estimated parameters
under different events may be different in the least-square error
based method proposed in [11]. Besides, Kalman ﬁlter based
methods have also been proposed for generator parameter cali-
bration based on PMU data [12]–[15]. However, these methods
usually suffer from slow convergence rate. In addition, the high
nonlinearity of the power system model may violate the local
linearity assumption for the extended Kalman ﬁlter (EKF)
based approach proposed in [12], [13].
More recently, Bayesian inference methods have been ap-
plied to perform generator parameter estimation [16]–[18].
The main disadvantage of Bayesian inference methods is
that an explicit likelihood function is needed which may
lead to computationally intractability. The accuracy of the
Bayesian method proposed in [16] degrades under poor prior
distributions of the parameters. The performance of surrogate-
based Bayesian inference method in [17] and the polynomial-
chaos-expansion-based Bayesian inference method in [18] may
deteriorate for high-dimensional parameters.
Besides, the multistage genetic algorithm optimization has
been proposed in [19] to estimate the generator parameters.
However, there is no guarantee of ﬁnding global optima and
the efﬁciency of the algorithm still needs to be improved. To
address these problems, in this paper we develop a black-box
optimization based generator parameter calibration method
based on a stochastic radial basis function (RBF) surrogate
model [20]. The proposed method does not require an explicit
objective function, can solve non-convex problems by building
a global model of the objective function, and guarantees con-
vergence to the global optimum from a theoretical standpoint
if the number of iterations is large enough [21].
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion II presents the synchronous generator dynamic model
used for model validation and parameter calibration. Section
III describes the sensitivity approach for identifying critical
parameters. Section IV discusses the black-box optimization

II. G ENERATOR DYNAMIC MODEL

ulates the model’s response. Fig. 1 illustrates the procedure
of model validation with event playback, where the PMU-
measured signals are played back to a subsystem model and
the simulated active/reactive power is compared with the
active/reactive power measured by PMUs. The external system
is modeled as a regulated voltage source and its voltage is
equal to the quantity measured by PMUs [13], [14].

III. I DENTIFYING CRITICAL PARAMETERS
After a model deﬁciency has been revealed, the next step
is to identify the problematic parameters. A generating unit
with its control can have many parameters. Calibrating all
of them could be computationally challenging and also not
every parameter is identiﬁable. Trajectory sensitivity has been
used to identify the most critical parameters [13]. Based
on trajectory sensitivities, we can have insights about how
the changes in parameters inﬂuence the system response.
Speciﬁcally, the sensitivity of the outputsP andQ with regard
to parameter αi can be calculated as [14]:

When the analytical expression of the objective function
is not known, the parameter estimation problem becomes a
black-box optimization problem. Many approaches have been
proposed for solving black-box optimization problems. Some
methods rely on metaheuristics, such as genetic algorithms
[23], particle swarm [23], and simulated annealing [24]. How-
ever, these methods suffer from slow convergence in many
applications [21]. Other methods based on direct search or
surrogate work faster than metaheuristics methods [20]. For
approximating a function for g, several methods have been
proposed. Trust region method builds local models for function
g [25]. In contrast, RBF method [26] and stochastic RBF
method [27] build a global model of function g [21].

During implementation, the algorithm should make a trade-
off between exploration and exploitation. Exploration implies
trying to improve the surrogate model in the unknown parts
of the parameter space, whereas exploitation implies trying

objective functions to a single objective function. For each

The points in the population with a large score are retained

A. Critical Parameter Identiﬁcation
Based on the trajectory sensitivity in Section III, it is found
that among 16 machine parameters only three parameters, the
d-axis transient rotor time constant (T pdo), inertia constant
(H), and d-axis synchronous reactance (x d) have considerable
effects on the model’s response. For the exciter with 18
parameters, only three parameters, the exciter gain (K A) and
time constants of the exciter (T c and Tb) are identiﬁed as
critical parameters. For the governor with 14 parameters,
only two parameters, the turbine coefﬁcient (a 23) and dashpot
time constant (T R) have considerable impacts on the model’s
response. The identiﬁed eight critical parameters and their
sensitivities are listed in Table II.

Based on [20], the performance of the thin-plate spline RBF
is better than the other types of RBFs. We thus choose thin-
plate spline as the RBF. We use RBFOpt [20] that implements
MSRSM and its parameters are set as default values. The
details about how to choose β can be found in [20]. The
maximum number of iterations T in Algorithm 1 is chosen
as 200 and 800, respectively, for estimating two and eight
critical parameters.
C. Validation under Different Prior Distributions
In this section, we analyze the estimation accuracy under
different prior information. We consider two parameters (the
moment of inertia H for synchronous generator and the
ampliﬁer gain KA for the exciter) with their true values as
H t = 5.4 andK t
A = 125. We choose the prior distributions as
uniform distribution with lower bound as 0 and upper bound
as 100% and 300% greater than the true values to account
for parameter uncertainties. The results for the parameter
estimation and the percentage errors are shown in Table IV.
It can be seen that the proposed method can provide accurate
estimation of the parameters under uniform prior distributions
with different settings.
We also choose the priors as uniform distributions whose
lower or upper bounds are very close to the true parameters.
As presented in Table V, even under these very extreme distri-
butions, the proposed approach still has a very high accuracy.
For the highlighted ﬁrst row in Table V, the prior distribution,
and the true and estimated values of the parameters are shown
in Fig. 2. It is seen that even when the true values are at the
tail regions of the assumed prior distributions, the proposed
algorithm can still very accurately estimate the parameters.
D. Validation for High Dimension
In this section, we perform parameter calibration for the
eight critical parameters. The prior of these parameters are
assumed to follow uniform distributions. The mean values of
the uniform distribution is set as 10% greater than their true
values. We choose the lower/upper bounds of the uniform prior
distributions as 30% smaller/greater than the mean values.
